text: This is TRACE, built for the ASUS UGen AI League.

Meet the station duty officer. One person, dozens of camera feeds, an alarm panel and a radio channel, all alerting separately. During the December 2025 attack on the Taipei Metro, forty-one detector groups fired across different zones, and operators had to piece the picture together, alarm by alarm.
Taipei Metro is now adding nearly three thousand AI cameras. Detection scales. Human attention doesn't.
TRACE is an edge copilot that turns that noise into one verified incident.

It runs on a single ASUS UGen300, a two and a half watt Hailo ten H stick that hosts four model families. YOLO watches every frame, Whisper listens to the radio, and only when the fusion engine sees a real incident does it wake Qwen2 VL for a second opinion. Video and audio never leave the box.
Here is the working prototype, replaying a run on openly licensed station footage.

An emergency intercom fires on Platform 2, and TRACE pulls snapshots from the nearby cameras. Eight seconds later a staff member radios in. Whisper transcribes the call on the device, and because the caller mentions exit C, the report lands in the adjacent zone.
Four systems, five signals, one high priority card, with a privacy masked clip, a timeline, and a summary where every sentence cites its source.
The officer can simply ask: anything near exit C? The on-device model answers from the event log only, with citations.

Now a crowd surge on Platform 1. Before anyone is alerted, the vision language model checks the scene, sees a train with passengers getting off, and keeps it low, writing its reasoning into the audit log. It can only downgrade camera-only alerts. It can never override an alarm or a human.
On the road, the same pipeline tracks fifty-five real scooters on Taipei Bridge, and flags one with repeated lateral swings, for review, never as a judgement about the rider.
One key press confirms, escalates or dismisses, and every decision is audited.

In a one-hour alert storm, four hundred and nine alarms become about nine high priority cards, while ninety-nine percent of real incidents are still caught. Per-sensor de-duplication alone removes only nine percent.
Every stage is timed today, and Stage Two moves each number onto the UGen300.
In Stage Two, we bring all four models up on one stick, run live cameras and radio, and test with real operators.
TRACE. From alarm noise, to one verified incident, at the edge.
